definition: Deciding which components a software system has, how they communicate and where its data lives, so that it meets its requirements for features, scale, speed, cost and reliability.
example: Choosing a load balancer, stateless app servers, a cache and a replicated database for a URL shortener is a system design.

definition: A statement of what a system must do: a behaviour a user or another system can observe, such as "given a long URL, return a short code".
example: "Users can upload a photo with a caption" is a functional requirement.

definition: A requirement about how well a system does its job rather than what it does: latency, throughput, availability, durability, scalability, security, cost. Good ones are measurable numbers, and they drive most architectural decisions.
example: "Redirect p99 latency under 50 ms" is a non-functional requirement.

definition: A fixed condition a design must work within and cannot change cheaply, such as team size and skills, a deadline, a budget, a regulation or an existing system to integrate with.
example: A team of three Python engineers with a four-month deadline is a constraint that favours managed services.

definition: A short, plain-language description of a feature from the user's point of view, typically "As a <user>, I want <goal> so that <reason>". Used to capture functional requirements.
example: "As a reader, I want to click a short link and land on the article" is a user story.

definition: Uniform Resource Locator: the address of a resource on the web, such as https://example.com/page. It names the protocol, the host and the path.
example: https://bit.ly/abc123 is a short URL that redirects to a much longer one.

definition: A service that maps a long URL to a short code and redirects anyone who visits the short code to the original URL. A classic system design exercise because it is simple to describe but read-heavy at scale.
example: Visiting /abc123 on the shortener returns a redirect to the original article URL.

definition: The brief identifier (for example abc123) that a URL shortener hands out in place of a long URL. Generating them without collisions across many servers is a classic design problem.
example: A 7-character base-62 code allows about 3.5 trillion distinct links.

definition: Writing a number using 62 symbols (0–9, a–z, A–Z) instead of 10 digits, which makes identifiers short and URL-safe. Each character carries about 5.95 bits.
example: 62 to the power 7 is about 3.5 trillion, so 7 base-62 characters cover trillions of IDs.

definition: An HTTP response (status 3xx) that tells the browser to go to a different URL, given in the Location header. URL shorteners answer every visit with one.
example: A 302 response with Location: https://example.com/article sends the browser on to the article.

definition: The three-digit number at the start of every HTTP response that says what happened: 2xx success, 3xx redirect, 4xx client error, 5xx server error.
example: 200 means OK, 404 means not found and 503 means the service is unavailable.

definition: An HTTP redirect status saying the resource has moved for good. Browsers may cache it heuristically (without explicit cache headers), so repeat visits can skip the server entirely.
example: After one 301 from a short link, a browser may go straight to the target next time, so the shortener never sees the click.

definition: An HTTP redirect status for a temporary move. Unlike 301 it is not cached by default, though explicit cache headers can still allow caching.
example: A URL shortener that counts clicks usually answers with 302 plus Cache-Control: no-store.

definition: An HTTP redirect status like 302, except the browser must repeat the request with the same method and body (a POST stays a POST).
example: A form submission redirected with 307 is re-sent as a POST to the new URL.

definition: An HTTP status saying the server cannot handle the request right now, usually because it is overloaded or down for maintenance. Clients should retry later, ideally with backoff.
example: A load-shedding server returns 503 to requests above its capacity.

definition: Any HTTP status from 500 to 599, meaning the server failed. Availability SLIs often count "non-5xx" responses as successes.
example: 500 Internal Server Error and 503 Service Unavailable are both 5xx responses.

definition: The HTTP method for reading a resource without changing it. It should be safe to repeat.
example: GET /abc123 asks the URL shortener where abc123 points.

definition: The HTTP method for sending data to the server, typically to create something. Repeating it may create duplicates unless the API is made idempotent.
example: POST /links with a long URL creates a new short link.

definition: The HTTP response header that carries the target URL of a redirect.
example: A 302 response includes Location: https://example.com/article.

definition: The HTTP header that tells browsers and intermediate caches whether and for how long a response may be cached. no-store forbids caching entirely.
example: Cache-Control: no-store on a redirect makes every click reach the server, so it can be counted.

definition: Caching a response that has no explicit freshness information because the HTTP rules allow it for certain status codes, such as 301. The cache guesses a reasonable lifetime.
example: A browser may keep a 301 redirect for days without being told to.

definition: How long a cached HTTP response may be reused without checking back with the server, set by headers such as Cache-Control: max-age.
example: Cache-Control: max-age=60 lets a cache reuse the response for 60 seconds.

definition: One URL plus HTTP method that an API exposes, such as POST /links. Clients call endpoints to use the service.
example: GET /links/{code}/stats is the endpoint that returns a link's click count.

definition: A server-side endpoint built for one client app that gathers data from several internal services and returns it in one response, so the client makes one call instead of many.
example: A mobile home screen that needed 12 calls can make 1 call to a BFF, which makes the 12 calls inside the datacentre.

definition: Recording and counting each visit to a link (when, from where, by what device) so owners can see usage. It turns every redirect into a write as well as a read.
example: At 12,000 redirects/s, click analytics adds 12,000 events/s to record.

definition: Search engine optimisation: making pages rank well in search results. Redirect status codes matter to it because search engines treat 301 as a permanent move.
example: Moving a page with a 301 tells search engines to transfer its ranking to the new URL.

definition: User interface: the screens, buttons and text a person interacts with. Styling choices in the UI rarely affect system architecture.
example: The colour of the shorten button is a UI decision, not a system design one.

definition: Portable Document Format: a file format for documents that look the same on any device. Ticketing systems often email tickets as PDFs.
example: Generating ticket PDFs is slow work best done by a background worker.

definition: The smallest version of a product that delivers enough value to real users to learn from. It should be built for modest scale with a path to grow.
example: An MVP marketplace expecting 50 orders a minute needs one managed database, not a Cassandra cluster.

definition: The fraction of time, or of requests, for which a system is able to serve correctly, usually written as a percentage such as 99.9%.
example: 99.9% availability allows about 43 minutes of downtime in a 30-day month.

definition: The guarantee that data, once stored or acknowledged, is not lost, even if machines crash or disks fail. It is about keeping data, not about being able to reach it right now.
example: Amazon S3 is designed for 99.999999999% (eleven nines) durability of objects over a year.

definition: The probability that a system works correctly without failure over a given period. A service with frequent brief failures can be highly available yet unreliable for long-running jobs.
example: A system that fails for 100 ms every minute is 99.8% available but breaks almost every hour-long job.

definition: A guarantee that once a write completes, every later read sees it (or something newer), as if there were a single copy. It usually costs coordination between replicas and therefore latency.
example: A bank balance read with strong consistency always reflects the last completed transfer.

definition: The rules a system with several copies of data (replicas, caches or processor cores) promises about which values reads may return after writes, from linearisability (strongest) through causal and read-your-writes to eventual consistency.
example: A store with read-your-writes guarantees you see your own edits but may show others' edits late.

definition: A system's ability to handle more load (requests, users, data, writes) by adding resources, while keeping performance acceptable and cost roughly proportional to load.
example: A stateless web tier is scalable: double the servers and it handles about double the requests.

definition: Daily active users: the number of distinct users who use a product on a given day. A standard starting point for estimating traffic.
example: 200 M DAU each posting twice a day gives 400 M posts a day.

definition: How many reads a system serves for each write. A high ratio (such as 100:1) favours caching and read replicas; a low one pushes towards partitioning writes.
example: A URL shortener with 4,000 redirects/s and 40 new links/s has a 100:1 read-to-write ratio.

definition: The highest load a system sees, usually in its busiest minutes, as opposed to the average. Capacity must cover the peak; peaks of 2–10 times the average are common.
example: An average of 4,000 requests/s with a peak factor of 3 means planning for 12,000 requests/s.

definition: Queries (or requests) per second: the standard unit of request rate. Average QPS is a daily count divided by about 86,400 seconds; capacity is planned for peak QPS.
example: 50 million events a day is about 579 QPS on average.

definition: A request rate: how many requests arrive or complete each second (req/min per minute). The same idea as QPS.
example: A server that saturates at 1,000 req/s should normally run well below that.

definition: In leader-based replication, the one database node that accepts writes and streams them to replicas. It is a common write bottleneck.
example: All 4,000 writes/s go to the Postgres primary, however many app servers you add.

definition: A copy of a database that follows the primary and serves reads, taking load off the primary. With asynchronous replication its data may lag slightly behind.
example: Adding two read replicas spreads 6,000 reads/s across three machines.

definition: A controlled, repeatable measurement of how a system performs under a defined workload and hardware. Capacity figures should come from benchmarks of your own workload, not generic numbers.
example: Benchmark the real queries at the target p99 before deciding how many writes/s one database can take.

definition: Grouping small operations so they share fixed costs such as a round trip or disk flush. This can improve throughput; waiting to form a batch can add latency, while reduced overhead or queueing can lower total latency.
example: Writing 50 rows in one INSERT instead of 50 separate statements saves 49 round trips.

definition: Competition between many workers for one shared resource (a lock, a database row, a disk), so they queue for it. In the Universal Scalability Law it is what makes throughput flatten.
example: Every request updating the same counter row creates contention on that row.

definition: Splitting a dataset into pieces stored on different machines, each holding a subset of the keys, so load and storage are spread. Called sharding when the pieces are separate databases.
example: Partitioning users by ID across 8 databases gives each about one-eighth of the writes.

definition: Storage that turns writes into appends at the end of a file instead of updates in place. Appends are sequential I/O, which disks handle far faster than random writes.
example: Kafka and LSM-tree databases are log-structured, which is why they ingest writes quickly.

definition: A geographic area where a cloud provider runs a cluster of datacentres, such as London or Virginia. Regions are far apart (tens to hundreds of milliseconds round trip) and fail independently.
example: Synchronously replicating between London and Virginia regions adds about 80 ms per write.

definition: One or more datacentres within a cloud region with independent power, cooling and networking. AWS places its zones up to about 100 km apart, close enough for single-digit-millisecond links. Spreading replicas across zones protects against one site failing.
example: With 25 servers in each of three zones, losing one leaves 50. They must have enough capacity for the required workload; zone separation alone does not guarantee continued service.

definition: The layer of servers that run the application code: they receive requests from the load balancer, apply business logic and call databases and caches. Usually kept stateless so it scales by adding servers.
example: A redirect hits the load balancer, then any app server, which checks the cache.

definition: The fraction of requests a cache answers itself without going to the slower store behind it. Every point of hit rate lost sends more load to the database.
example: At a 95% hit rate the database sees 5% of reads; at 90% it sees twice as many.

definition: A request the cache cannot answer because it does not hold the item, so the item must be fetched from the slower store behind it. Also used for CPU caches, where a miss means a trip to main memory.
example: With the cache cluster down, every read becomes a cache miss.

definition: A single key (one link, one user, one product) that receives a disproportionate share of traffic and so overloads whichever server or partition holds it.
example: One viral link receiving 50,000 reads/s is a hot key for the shard that stores it.

definition: The subset of data that is accessed often enough to be worth keeping in a cache. Sizing a cache means measuring the hot set, not the whole dataset.
example: 80 million frequently visited links of 500 bytes form a 40 GB hot set.

definition: An open-source system for running containers across a cluster of machines: it schedules them, restarts failed ones and scales them. Powerful but operationally demanding to run yourself.
example: Self-managing Kubernetes, Kafka and Cassandra is a lot for a three-person team.

definition: An open-source, distributed wide-column database that spreads data across many nodes with no single leader. It offers tunable consistency per request and is built for high write volumes.
example: Discord stored billions of messages in Cassandra for years.

definition: Infrastructure (a database, queue, search engine) run for you by a provider, who handles provisioning, patching, backups and failover. You trade control and some cost for far less operational work.
example: Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL is a managed database: no one on your team patches the server.

definition: An application deployed as a single unit, with all its features in one codebase and process. Simpler to build, test and operate than microservices; a modular monolith keeps clear internal boundaries.
example: A team of seven can usually ship faster with one well-structured monolith than with 12 services.

definition: A set of microservices so tightly coupled (shared database, lock-step deploys) that they have the costs of distribution without the independence benefit.
example: Twelve services that all read and write the same database tables form a distributed monolith.

definition: Being the engineer responsible for responding to production alerts at any hour during a rota. Every component you run adds to the on-call burden.
example: An alert at 3 a.m. pages the on-call engineer, who must diagnose and fix the outage.

definition: A queue placed in front of a busy flow (such as ticket checkout) that admits users at a rate the backend can sustain and shows the rest their place in line.
example: When 10,000 users/s arrive for a tour, a waiting room releases 1,500/s to checkout.

definition: Deciding at the entrance how much work to accept, so a system is never asked to do more than it can; excess work is queued or rejected up front instead of overloading everything.
example: Admitting 1,500 checkouts/s keeps a 2,000/s inventory store healthy during a spike.

definition: A write that succeeds only if the stored data still meets a condition, checked atomically, such as "set holder only if the seat has no holder". It prevents two writers both succeeding.
example: UPDATE seats SET holder=? WHERE id=? AND holder IS NULL is a conditional write.

definition: An operation that happens completely or not at all, with no other operation able to see or interleave with a half-done state.
example: Redis INCR is atomic: two clients incrementing at once always add 2.

definition: Deliberately rejecting some requests (often with a quick error) when overloaded, so the requests that are accepted still succeed instead of everything slowing to a halt.
example: Returning 503 to traffic above 2,000/s is load shedding.

definition: A surge of load caused by many clients retrying failed requests at once, which keeps an already struggling service overloaded.
example: If every client retries a 503 immediately, a 5x overload can become a 10x overload.

definition: Retrying after waits that grow each time (for example 100 ms, 200 ms, 400 ms), usually with random jitter, so retries do not all land at once.
example: With backoff, a client's fourth retry waits 800 ms instead of hammering the server.

definition: Sending a request again after it failed or timed out. Useful for brief glitches, but it multiplies load during outages and is only safe for idempotent operations.
example: Three layers each retrying three times can turn 1 request into 27.

definition: Merging many simultaneous requests for the same missing item into one fetch from the backend, whose result is shared by all of them.
example: 1,000 requests for a just-expired key trigger one database query instead of 1,000.

definition: A service that stores user identities and authenticates them for other applications, for example via single sign-on.
example: Employees log in through the company identity provider rather than a separate password for each tool.

aliases: Payment Card Industry Data Security Standard
definition: The Payment Card Industry Data Security Standard: security rules for any system that stores, processes or transmits payment card data.
example: Keeping card numbers out of your own systems by using a payment provider shrinks your PCI DSS scope.

definition: The EU General Data Protection Regulation: law governing how personal data of people in the EU is processed, including transfers to other countries.
example: GDPR is why many companies keep EU customers' data in EU regions.

definition: A rule about which country or region data may be stored or processed in, set by law or company policy.
example: An EU-only residency policy rules out replicating customer data to a US region.

definition: The stage of a design discussion that examines the hardest parts of a specific system in detail: ID generation, consistency, failure handling, hot keys.
example: A deep dive on a URL shortener asks what happens when the cache cluster fails.

definition: The one resource that limits the throughput of the whole system; improving anything else does not help until it is relieved.
example: If the database saturates at 4,000 writes/s, it is the bottleneck however many app servers you add.

definition: A decision where gaining one property means giving up some of another, such as lower latency for weaker consistency. Good designs state their trade-offs explicitly.
example: Acknowledging writes before replication trades durability for latency.

definition: A specific way a component or system can fail (crash, slow down, return wrong data, lose connectivity), and what happens as a result.
example: A cache failing is a failure mode that sends every read to the database.

definition: A component whose failure alone takes the whole system down, because nothing else can take over its job.
example: One database server with no replica is a single point of failure.

definition: Unused capacity deliberately kept in reserve so a system can absorb bursts, growth or the loss of a server without overloading.
example: Running at 60% peak utilisation leaves 40% headroom.

definition: Working out how many servers, how much storage and how much bandwidth a system needs to meet its targets at expected peak load, with headroom.
example: Capacity planning for 45,000 req/s at 60% utilisation gives 75 servers of 1,000 req/s each.

definition: The fraction of time a resource (CPU, disk, server) is busy, from 0% to 100%. Queueing delay grows sharply as it approaches 100%.
example: A server busy 900 ms of every second is at 90% utilisation.

definition: The sequence of components a single request passes through, from client to data store and back. Walking through it is a quick way to find missing pieces in a design.
example: Client → load balancer → app server → cache → read replica is the redirect request flow.

definition: How a system's data is organised: the entities, their fields and the relationships between them, and how they are stored and keyed.
example: A link table with code, long URL, owner and created time is a URL shortener's data model.

definition: Running a piece of infrastructure (a database, Kafka, Kubernetes) on servers your own team operates, rather than as a managed service. More control and sometimes lower cost at scale, much more operational work.
example: Self-hosting log search can be cheaper than a vendor at 200 TB a month, if the team can operate it.

definition: The authoritative record of what is available to sell (seats, stock items). It must never be decremented twice for the same unit, so it needs strong consistency.
example: Selling the last seat must use an atomic conditional write against the inventory.

definition: Selling more units than exist (or the same seat twice), typically because two buyers read a stale "available" value and both succeeded.
example: Two checkouts reading "1 left" from stale replicas can both succeed and oversell.

definition: One thousandth of a second (0.001 s). The usual unit for network and request latency.
example: A round trip inside a datacentre takes about 0.5 ms; London to New York about 70 ms.

definition: One millionth of a second (0.000001 s), a thousandth of a millisecond. Used for fast storage and memory operations.
example: A random 4 KB read from an SSD takes roughly 20–150 µs.

definition: One billionth of a second (0.000000001 s). Used for CPU cache and memory access times.
example: A main-memory reference takes around 100 ns.

definition: Glass cable that carries data as pulses of light. Light travels through it at about 200,000 km/s, roughly two-thirds of its speed in a vacuum, which sets a hard floor on long-distance latency.
example: Light needs at least 28 ms to cross the 5,570 km from London to New York in fibre.

definition: The time a signal takes just to travel from one point to another: across a network link it is the distance divided by the signal speed, and no amount of bandwidth or extra servers reduces it.
example: A 5,570 km fibre path has about 28 ms of one-way propagation delay.

definition: The shortest distance between two points on the surface of a sphere such as the Earth, measured along the surface. Real cables are longer.
example: The great-circle distance from London to New York is about 5,570 km.

definition: Amazon's cloud computing platform, offering servers (EC2), storage (S3), databases (DynamoDB, RDS) and many other services by the hour or by usage.
example: AWS publishes availability commitments (SLAs) for each service.

definition: A former AWS service that moved up to 100 PB of data by lorry in a shipping-container-sized storage unit; AWS withdrew it in 2024. A vivid example of huge throughput with huge latency.
example: Snowmobile could move 100 PB in weeks, faster than most network links.

definition: A rugged storage device AWS ships to customers to move large amounts of data physically. AWS stopped accepting new Snowball Edge customers on 7 November 2025 and has announced the end of support for Snowball devices in its commercial Regions on 31 December 2026.
example: Copying 80 TB to a Snowball Edge and posting it can beat a slow uplink.

definition: Requests waiting for a busy resource. Waiting time adds to latency and grows sharply as utilisation approaches 100%; queueing theory is the maths that models it.
example: A server at 90% utilisation makes requests wait about 9 times their service time in the M/M/1 model.

definition: The simplest queueing model: random (Poisson) arrivals, randomly (exponentially) distributed service times and one server. Its average time in system is the service time divided by (1 − utilisation).
example: With a 10 ms service time at 90% load, an M/M/1 queue predicts 100 ms average latency.

definition: How long a server spends actually working on one request, excluding any time the request waits in a queue.
example: A request with 10 ms of service time can take 100 ms in total on a busy server.

definition: How many requests (or items) enter a system per unit time, usually per second. Written λ (lambda) in queueing formulas.
example: A service receiving 2,000 requests every second has an arrival rate of 2,000/s.

definition: The long-run behaviour of a system once start-up effects have passed and averages stop changing. For example, a queue only reaches a steady state if requests arrive more slowly than they can be served.
example: At or above 100% utilisation a queue never reaches a steady state; it just keeps growing.

definition: For any stable system, the average number of items inside equals the average arrival rate multiplied by the average time each item spends inside (L = λ × W). It holds whatever the pattern of arrivals.
example: 2,000 requests/s each taking 50 ms means about 100 requests in flight.

definition: Having several operations in progress over the same period, not necessarily executing at the same instant; also the number of operations in progress at once. Little's law links that number to throughput and latency.
example: 100 requests in flight means 100 are being handled or waiting at once.

definition: Describes a transfer whose time is dominated by pushing bytes through the link (size ÷ bandwidth) rather than by round trips. A faster link or compression helps.
example: Copying a 10 GB file over 1 Gbps takes about 80 s, nearly all of it data transfer.

definition: Describes work whose time is dominated by waiting for replies rather than transmitting bytes. Avoiding or overlapping independent exchanges, or moving work closer, usually helps more than increasing bandwidth.
example: For 1,000 sequential calls with an assumed 80 ms round trip, network waiting alone is about 80 seconds.

definition: A message going to another machine and its reply coming back. Each sequential round trip adds one RTT of latency.
example: A London app making 12 sequential calls to the US pays 12 round trips of 70 ms.

definition: Doing several pieces of work at the same time on different workers, cores or machines, to finish sooner or handle more.
example: Sending 10 independent calls in parallel takes about one round trip instead of ten.

definition: A limit on how long a caller waits for a response before giving up. Timeouts stop slow dependencies tying up threads forever.
example: A 200 ms timeout on a recommendations call lets the page render without them if that service stalls.

definition: A threshold locating a chosen fraction of sorted measurements. For latency, p99 is a threshold with roughly 99% of requests at or below it; ties, interpolation and the measurement method matter. p50 describes the median.
example: A p99 near 300 ms locates the slow end of the distribution; it does not imply exactly 1% exceed 300 ms when observations tie.

definition: The middle value when measurements are sorted (the 50th percentile, p50): half are at or below it. It describes the typical case and is not dragged around by outliers.
example: For 98 requests at 10 ms and 2 at 2,000 ms, the median is 10 ms.

definition: The sum of all values divided by how many there are. A few very slow requests can pull it far from any real request's latency.
example: Latencies of 98 × 10 ms and 2 × 2,000 ms have a mean of 49.8 ms, which no request actually took.

definition: The latency of the slowest requests, at high percentiles such as p99 and p99.9. It matters because heavy users and fan-out requests hit it often.
example: A service with p50 of 20 ms may still have a tail latency of 900 ms at p99.9.

definition: The symmetric, bell-shaped probability distribution where values cluster around the mean. Latency distributions are usually not normal: they have a long right tail.
example: Human heights are roughly normally distributed; request latencies are not.

definition: A moment when a program stops running application code so the garbage collector can reclaim memory. Pauses of tens of milliseconds to seconds are a common source of tail latency.
example: A 20-second GC pause looks to other nodes exactly like a network partition.

definition: Sending a network packet again because the first copy was lost or not acknowledged in time; TCP does it automatically, at the cost of extra delay.
example: A lost packet that TCP retransmits after 200 ms adds 200 ms to that request.

definition: Another workload sharing the same physical machine, disk or network that slows yours down by consuming shared resources.
example: A batch job on the same host saturating the disk makes your database reads slow.

definition: Amazon's internal highly available key-value store, described in a 2007 paper. It chose availability during failures and merged conflicting versions, and inspired Cassandra and others.
example: Dynamo merged conflicting shopping carts by taking the union of their items.

definition: One request triggering many parallel requests to other servers (for example one per shard), then waiting for the replies. The overall request is as slow as the slowest reply.
example: A search fanning out to 100 shards is slow whenever any one shard is slow.

definition: A number from 0 (impossible) to 1 (certain) saying how likely an event is; 0.01 means 1 time in 100.
example: If each server is slow with probability 0.01, it is fast with probability 0.99.

definition: Failures (or events) are independent when one happening does not change the chance of another. Only then can you multiply their probabilities, as the availability formulas do.
example: Two servers on separate power supplies fail roughly independently; two in the same rack do not.

definition: The probability that an event does not happen: 1 minus the probability that it does. Often the easy way to compute "at least one".
example: The chance at least one of 50 shards is slow is 1 minus the chance all 50 are fast.

definition: A 2013 paper by Jeffrey Dean and Luiz André Barroso of Google explaining why tail latency dominates in large fan-out systems and how to tolerate it (hedged and tied requests, reducing variability).
example: The paper reports hedging cutting a p99.9 from 1,800 ms to 74 ms for 2% more requests.

definition: Sending a duplicate of a slow request to another replica after a short delay (often the p95 time) and using whichever reply arrives first. It cuts tail latency for a few percent extra load.
example: If 40 ms is the p95 latency, hedging after 40 ms sends only about 5% of requests twice.

definition: A duplicate request sent to two servers at once, each told about the other, so that when one starts processing it cancels its twin.
example: Tied requests avoid doing the duplicated work twice.

definition: A count of how many measurements fall in each range (bucket) of values. Histograms from many servers can be added together and percentiles computed from the total; percentiles themselves cannot be averaged.
example: Summing each server's 0–10 ms, 10–50 ms and 50–100 ms bucket counts gives the fleet histogram.

definition: An open-source histogram library designed to record latencies with fixed relative precision across a huge range, and to merge histograms accurately.
example: Record every request into an HdrHistogram, then merge them across hosts.

definition: An open-source monitoring system that stores metrics as time series. Its histogram metrics can be summed across servers and turned into percentiles with histogram_quantile.
example: histogram_quantile(0.99, sum(rate(bucket[5m])) by (le)) gives a fleet-wide p99.

definition: A load-testing error where the tester stops sending while the server is stalled, so the requests that would have suffered the stall are never measured and the tail looks better than it is.
example: During a 1 s stall, ten closed-loop clients record about 10 slow requests, while a target rate of 1,000 req/s should have recorded about 1,000.

definition: Sending controlled, realistic traffic at a system to measure its latency and throughput and find its limits before real users do.
example: A load test at 1,000 req/s should show the p99 you will see in production.

definition: An HTTP load-testing tool that sends requests at a constant rate regardless of responses (open loop), avoiding coordinated omission.
example: wrk2 -R 1000 sends 1,000 requests per second however slowly the server answers.

definition: A load tester that sends requests on a fixed schedule whether or not earlier ones have been answered, as real independent users do.
example: An open-loop test keeps sending during a stall, so every delayed request is recorded.

definition: A load tester whose clients each wait for a response before sending the next request, so it slows down whenever the server does and under-reports stalls.
example: Ten closed-loop clients send nothing new during a 1 s server stall.

definition: Small, very fast memory on the processor that holds recently used data. L1 is smallest and fastest (about 1 ns); L2 and L3 are larger and slower; main memory is about 100 times slower than L1.
example: Data laid out contiguously stays in L1 and L2 cache and is processed much faster.

definition: When the processor guesses the wrong way at an if-statement and must throw away work it started speculatively, costing a few nanoseconds.
example: A hard-to-predict branch in a hot loop can cost 3–5 ns each time it guesses wrong.

definition: The computer's RAM, which holds running programs and their data. Much faster than any disk, much slower than CPU caches.
example: A main-memory reference takes around 100 ns.

definition: A fast compression library from Google that favours speed over compression ratio.
example: Compressing 1 KB with Snappy takes about 2 µs.

definition: Storage built from flash memory chips with no moving parts. Random reads take tens to hundreds of microseconds, far faster than a spinning disk.
example: A random 4 KB SSD read takes roughly 20–150 µs.

definition: Storage that records data on spinning magnetic platters read by a moving head. Sequential reads are reasonably fast, but each random access needs a seek of several milliseconds.
example: An HDD seek of about 10 ms is 20 times a datacentre round trip.

definition: Moving a hard disk's read head to the right track and waiting for the data to rotate under it, typically several milliseconds. It is why random I/O on HDDs is slow.
example: Reading 100 scattered blocks costs 100 seeks, about 1 s on an HDD.

definition: Reading or writing data in consecutive order. Disks (especially HDDs) do this far faster than random access because no seeks are needed.
example: An HDD can stream 100+ MB/s sequentially but only about 100 random reads a second.

definition: Reading or writing small pieces of data at scattered locations. Each access may need a seek, so it is much slower than sequential I/O on disks.
example: A random 4 KB read costs about 10 ms on an HDD.

definition: Any transfer of data between a program and the outside world: disk reads and writes, network traffic and so on. It is usually far slower than computation.
example: A database waiting on disk reads is I/O-bound.

definition: A building full of servers, storage and networking with its own power and cooling. Round trips inside one take about half a millisecond.
example: Moving 12 chatty calls inside the datacentre turns 840 ms into about 76 ms.

definition: Replication where a write is acknowledged only after it has reached one or more replicas, so an acknowledged write survives losing the primary. Each write pays a round trip to the replica.
example: Synchronous replication from London to Virginia makes every write take at least 80 ms.

definition: Replication where the primary acknowledges a write before replicas have it and ships it to them afterwards. Fast, but replicas lag and a crash can lose the latest writes.
example: An async replica in Sydney may show a profile edit a second or two after it was saved in Virginia.

definition: An interaction that needs many small sequential exchanges to get one job done. Over long distances, its cost is dominated by round trips.
example: 20 sequential calls at 70 ms each take 1.4 s.

definition: A network speed of 10^9 bits per second. Divide by 8 to get bytes: 1 Gbps is 125 MB/s.
example: A 10 Gbps network card can send at most about 1.25 GB/s.

definition: A data rate of 10^6 bits per second. Video streams and home broadband are usually quoted in Mbps.
example: An HD video stream averages a few Mbps; 5 Mbps is 625 KB/s.

definition: A data rate of 10^12 bits per second, the scale of a large video service's total peak traffic.
example: A million viewers at 5 Mbps need 5 Tbps.

definition: The smallest unit of data: a single 0 or 1. Network speeds are counted in bits per second.
example: A byte is 8 bits, so 8,000 bits is 1,000 bytes.

definition: A unit of data made of 8 bits, enough for one character of plain text. Storage and file sizes are counted in bytes.
example: A 500-byte record holds a short code, a URL and some timestamps.

definition: In estimation, 1,000 bytes (strictly a KiB is 1,024). A short text post with metadata is about 1 KB.
example: A million 1 KB rows is 1 GB.

definition: One million (10^6) bytes in decimal units. A compressed photo is often 0.2–2 MB.
example: 1 MB/s sustained adds up to about 30 TB a year.

definition: One billion (10^9) bytes in decimal units. Server RAM and cache sizes are usually quoted in GB.
example: An 80-million-entry hot set of 500-byte records is 40 GB.

definition: One trillion (10^12) bytes, a thousand gigabytes. Large database disks are a few TB.
example: 12 billion records of 500 bytes is 6 TB.

definition: One quadrillion (10^15) bytes, a thousand terabytes. Photo and video services store many petabytes.
example: 20 TB of photos a day is about 7.3 PB a year.

definition: Units based on powers of 2: a KiB is 1,024 bytes, a MiB 1,024 KiB, a GiB 1,024 MiB. They differ from decimal KB/MB/GB by 2.4% at KB, growing to about 13% at PB.
example: A "16 GB" RAM stick holds 16 GiB, about 17.2 billion bytes.

definition: Some number of copies of ten multiplied together, written 10^n: a 1 followed by n zeros. Writing big numbers this way makes estimation arithmetic a matter of adding and subtracting exponents.
example: 10^5 is 100,000, roughly the seconds in a day.

definition: The small raised number in x^n saying how many copies of x to multiply together. 0.99^50 means 50 copies of 0.99 multiplied together.
The logarithm to base e (about 2.718): ln(x) is the power you must raise e to in order to get x. It turns powers into multiplications, which makes things like 0.99^50 easy to estimate.
The mathematical constant e ≈ 2.71828, the base of natural logarithms. It appears whenever growth or decay compounds continuously.
Rounding a number up to the next whole number, written ⌈x⌉. A whole number stays as it is.
Rounding a number down to the whole number below, written ⌊x⌋. A whole number stays as it is.
example: ⌊5 / 2⌋ = ⌊2.5⌋ = 2, so a majority of 5 is 2 + 1 = 3.

definition: A factor of about ten. Two numbers are an order of magnitude apart if one is roughly ten times the other; estimation aims to get the order of magnitude right.
example: 100 ns and 100 µs are three orders of magnitude apart.

definition: The time a system is running and serving correctly. Time-based availability is uptime divided by total time.
example: 43,157 minutes of uptime in a 43,200-minute month is 99.9% availability.

definition: The time a system is unavailable. An availability target fixes how much downtime per month or year is allowed.
example: 99.99% allows about 52.6 minutes of downtime a year.

definition: Shorthand for availability or durability percentages by counting the 9s: three nines is 99.9%, four nines 99.99%. Each extra nine cuts allowed downtime by a factor of 10.
example: Five nines (99.999%) allows about 26 seconds of downtime a month.

definition: The amount of failure an SLO allows: 1 minus the target. Teams spend it on releases and experiments and slow down when it runs out.
example: A 99.9% SLO over 30 days gives an error budget of about 43 minutes.

definition: A measured number describing how a service is doing, such as the proportion of requests that succeed within 300 ms.
example: "99.95% of requests returned non-5xx in under 300 ms this week" reports an SLI.

definition: An internal target for an SLI over a period, such as 99.9% of requests succeeding over 30 days. It sets the error budget.
example: An SLO of 99.9% monthly availability allows 43 minutes of downtime.

definition: A contract with customers promising a service level, with consequences such as service credits if it is missed. Usually looser than the internal SLO.
example: AWS's EC2 region-level SLA promises 99.99% under its stated conditions.

definition: An approach to running production systems, created at Google, that treats operations as a software problem and manages reliability with SLOs and error budgets.
example: The Google SRE book argues against 100% availability targets.

definition: Components a request needs all of, one after another. Their availabilities multiply, so the chain is less available than its weakest link.
example: A load balancer (99.99%), app (99.9%) and database (99.95%) in series give about 99.84%.

definition: Redundant components where any one can do the job, so the group fails only if all fail. Availability is 1 minus the product of their down-fractions.
example: Two independent 99% servers in parallel give 99.99%.

definition: The chain of steps that must each finish, one after another, before a result is ready, so it sets the minimum total time. In a request path, anything on it adds its latency and its failures to every request.
example: Moving analytics writes off the critical path means analytics outages no longer break redirects.

definition: A call where the caller waits for the answer before carrying on. The caller's latency and availability then include the callee's.
example: A checkout that synchronously calls 6 services is down whenever any of them is.

definition: Handing work to be done later (often through a queue) instead of waiting for it, so the caller can respond immediately and is shielded from the worker's failures.
example: Emailing tickets asynchronously lets checkout finish even if the email service is slow.

definition: Continuing to provide the core function, with reduced features, when a part of the system fails, rather than failing completely.
example: Showing a product page without recommendations when the recommender is down is graceful degradation.

definition: Having more than one component able to do the same job, so the system survives one of them failing.
example: Two load balancers and three app servers give the tier redundancy.

definition: Provisioning enough capacity (N) to meet peak load plus at least one spare unit, so losing one server or zone still leaves enough. N+2 keeps two spares.
example: If peak needs 4 servers, N+1 means running 5.

definition: Switching service from a failed component to a standby. It takes time (detect, decide, promote, redirect traffic), which counts as downtime.
example: A 15-minute failover four times a year is an hour of downtime.

definition: A redundant group that works as long as at least k of its n members are up, for example when any two of three servers can carry peak load.
example: Three 99% servers needing any two give 99.97%.

definition: A frame holding many servers that typically share a power feed and a top-of-rack network switch, so they can all fail together.
example: Two replicas in the same rack both go offline if its switch dies.

definition: Several components failing together because of a shared cause (power, a bug, a bad config), which breaks the independence the availability formulas assume.
example: A config push that crashes every replica at once is a correlated failure.

definition: An extra second occasionally added to clock time to keep it aligned with the Earth's rotation. Mishandling it has crashed whole fleets of identical servers at once.
example: The 2012 leap second triggered bugs that took down several large websites.

definition: Rolling out a changed configuration to running servers. A bad push to all servers at once is a common cause of correlated outages.
example: Pushing a config to one zone first limits the damage if it is wrong.

definition: Releasing a change to a small fraction of servers or users first, then widening it only if nothing breaks.
example: Deploying to 1% of servers, then 10%, then 100% is a staged rollout.

definition: A set of components that can all be taken out by one failure, such as a rack, a zone or a region. Redundancy should span failure domains.
example: Replicas in three zones sit in three separate failure domains.

definition: Deliberately injecting failures (killing servers, cutting links) in a controlled way to check that redundancy and failover really work. A game day is a planned exercise of this kind.
example: A game day that fails over the primary database proves the standby works.

definition: A replica kept ready to take over if the primary fails. It must be tested regularly to be trusted.
example: Promoting the standby after the primary dies restores writes in minutes.

definition: The average time a repairable system runs between failures. Raising it (fewer failures) is one of the two levers on availability.
example: A server that fails on average every 1,000 hours has an MTBF of 1,000 h.

definition: The average time from a failure to restored service: detect, diagnose, fix, verify. Cutting it is often the cheapest way to raise availability.
example: Automated failover cutting MTTR from 2 hours to 6 minutes lifts availability from 99.72% to 99.986%.

definition: The average time until a non-repairable part fails, such as a disk that is replaced rather than fixed.
example: A disk with a rated MTTF of 1 million hours still fails sometimes in a large fleet.

definition: The average time from a failure starting until someone or something notices it. The first part of MTTR.
example: Alerting on error rate rather than on a weekly report cuts MTTD from days to minutes.

definition: A written, step-by-step procedure for handling a known operational task or incident, so whoever is on call can act quickly.
example: The runbook for "primary database down" lists how to check and promote the standby.

definition: Undoing a change to return to an earlier good state, such as reverting a bad deploy or configuration to the previous version. In databases the same word means abandoning a transaction's changes.
example: A one-click rollback undoes a broken deploy in a minute.

definition: Automatically notifying engineers when monitored metrics show a problem. Alerting on user-facing symptoms (errors, latency) catches real problems fastest.
example: An alert fires when the error rate exceeds 1% for 5 minutes.

definition: Recording the path and timing of each request through every service it touches, so you can see where time went and what failed.
example: A trace shows that 900 ms of a 1 s request was spent waiting on one shard.

definition: A screen of graphs showing a system's key metrics in real time, used to spot and diagnose problems.
example: A dashboard showing p99 latency per server makes one degraded host obvious.

definition: A refund or discount a provider owes customers when it misses an SLA.
example: Missing a 99.99% SLA might earn customers a 10% service credit.

definition: Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud: AWS's service for renting virtual servers (instances) by the second or hour.
example: Running app servers on EC2 instances in three availability zones.

definition: Amazon Simple Storage Service: AWS's object storage, designed for 99.999999999% durability. Used for files, images, backups and data lakes.
example: Photos go into S3 while the database keeps a 1 KB metadata row per photo.

definition: Storage that keeps whole files ("objects") under keys over HTTP, scaling to huge sizes cheaply. Ideal for blobs such as photos and videos; not a database.
example: Store a 2 MB photo in object storage and its URL in the database.

definition: Keeping previous versions of a stored object when it is overwritten or deleted, so accidental changes can be undone. It does not help when the service itself is unreachable.
example: With S3 versioning on, a deleted file can be restored from its earlier version.

definition: The part of a system that manages configuration and coordination (creating resources, routing changes), as opposed to the data plane that serves the actual traffic.
example: A control-plane outage can stop you creating buckets while existing reads still work.

definition: A redundancy setup where one site or server handles traffic and another waits idle to take over after a failover.
example: An active-passive pair of regions pays failover time on every incident.

definition: A redundancy setup where several sites or servers all handle traffic at once, so losing one just shifts load to the others with no promotion step.
example: Active-active regions avoid a 15-minute failover but need conflict handling for writes.

definition: How long DNS answers may be cached by resolvers and clients. A low TTL makes a DNS-based failover take effect sooner.
example: With a 60 s TTL, clients follow a DNS change within about a minute.

definition: Handling more load by moving to a bigger machine (more CPU, RAM, faster disks). Simple and needs no code changes, but has a ceiling and remains a single point of failure.
example: Moving Postgres from 16 to 32 vCPUs is vertical scaling.

definition: Handling more load by adding more machines and spreading work across them. Near-unlimited if the work partitions well, but brings load balancing and distributed-data problems.
example: Adding 10 more stateless app servers behind the load balancer is horizontal scaling.

definition: A virtual CPU: one unit of processor capacity in a cloud server, usually one hardware thread of a physical core.
example: A 16-vCPU instance at 70% load is using about 11 vCPUs of work.

definition: One independent processing unit inside a CPU, able to run one thread of work at a time (or two with hyper-threading).
example: 1,000 CPU-seconds of work arriving every second keep 1,000 cores busy.

definition: A virtual server rented from a cloud provider. Its type fixes its CPU, memory and network capacity.
example: Moving to a larger instance type doubles RAM without code changes.

definition: A cheap cloud server using spare capacity that the provider can reclaim at short notice. Only suitable for workloads that tolerate being killed at any moment.
example: Stateless workers on spot instances can cost far less than on-demand ones.

definition: Automatically adding or removing servers as load changes, based on metrics such as CPU. It reacts in minutes, not instantly.
example: An autoscaling group grows from 10 to 30 servers as morning traffic rises.

definition: Ordinary, widely available, inexpensive servers rather than specialist high-end machines. Horizontal scaling uses many of them.
example: A cluster of 100 commodity servers replaces one huge machine.

definition: How services find the current network addresses of the instances of other services, which change as instances start, stop and move.
example: A new app instance registers itself so the load balancer starts sending it traffic.

definition: A system whose components run on several networked machines and coordinate by sending messages. It can survive single-machine failures but must cope with network delays and partitions.
example: A database replicated across three zones is a distributed system.

definition: A service whose correctness does not depend on client state kept only in one instance between requests. Authoritative state lives in appropriate backing services or request data, so another instance can handle the next request; safe replacement still needs capacity, retry handling and graceful shutdown.
example: An app tier that stores sessions in Redis rather than in memory is stateless.

definition: A component that holds data that matters between requests (a database, a cache, a WebSocket server), so which instance handles a request matters and scaling it needs partitioning and replication.
example: A WebSocket server is stateful: killing it drops its users' connections.

definition: A load balancer routing each user's requests to the same server so in-memory state there keeps working. A stop-gap: the state is lost if that server dies.
example: Sticky sessions hide in-memory sessions until a server restart logs everyone out.

definition: Data a server keeps about a logged-in user between requests, such as their identity. Where it is stored decides whether the app tier is stateless.
example: Storing sessions in Redis lets any of 4 servers recognise the user.

definition: A widely used set of 12 principles for building cloud services; one is that processes are stateless and share nothing, keeping state in backing services.
example: Reading config from environment variables is a Twelve-Factor recommendation.

definition: Any service an app uses over the network (database, cache, queue, object store) to hold state or do work, treated as an attached resource.
example: Postgres and Redis are backing services of a stateless web app.

definition: A server that receives messages from producers, stores them and delivers them to consumers, decoupling the two. Kafka and RabbitMQ are examples.
example: A Kafka broker holds the order events until each consumer reads them.

definition: Moving data or work between nodes when nodes join, leave or fail, so load stays even.
example: Adding a fourth node triggers rebalancing of a quarter of the partitions onto it.

definition: The architecture habit of keeping state in a few dedicated, well-understood stateful systems (databases, caches, queues, object stores) so everything above them can be stateless.
example: Moving uploads from local disk to S3 pushes state down.

definition: The rule that the serial (non-parallelisable) part of a task limits the speed-up from adding workers: with serial fraction s, the speed-up can never exceed 1 / s.
example: A job that is 5% serial can never run more than 20 times faster.

definition: The share of a job that must run one step at a time and cannot be split across workers. It caps speed-up in Amdahl's law.
example: A 10-minute merge in a 100-minute job is a serial fraction of 0.1.

definition: How many times faster a job runs after a change, such as adding workers or faster hardware: the old running time divided by the new.
example: Cutting a 100-minute job to 19 minutes is a 5.3x speed-up.

definition: A single lock that every request must take, so work through it happens one at a time however many servers you add.
example: A global lock around ID generation becomes the serial bottleneck at high write rates.

definition: A component that assigns a single global order (sequence numbers) to events. If it is one process, it caps throughput.
example: A single-threaded sequencer stamping every trade limits an exchange to what one core can do.

definition: A service that directs or orders the work of others. If there is only one, it can become a bottleneck and a single point of failure.
example: A single coordinator assigning every job to workers caps throughput.

definition: Neil Gunther's model of how throughput scales with nodes, adding contention (which flattens the curve) and coherence costs (which can make it fall) to Amdahl's law.
example: A throughput curve that rises then falls fits the USL with a coherence term.

definition: Coherence is keeping several copies of shared data (in CPU caches or on different nodes) consistent with each other. In the Universal Scalability Law, its cost grows roughly with the number of node pairs, so it can make throughput fall as nodes are added.
example: Broadcasting every cache invalidation to every other node is a coherence cost.

definition: Keeping copies of the same data in several caches (CPU caches or nodes' caches) consistent with each other, which needs messages between them.
example: When one core writes a value, cache coherence invalidates the copies in other cores' caches.

definition: Telling every node to drop its cached copy of an item when the item changes. With N nodes each broadcasting to all others, traffic grows roughly with N squared.
example: 16 nodes broadcasting to each other create 120 node pairs of chatter.

definition: The optimistic counterpart to Amdahl's law: as you add workers you usually also grow the problem, so the parallel part grows and scaling stays worthwhile.
example: Ten times the machines can process ten times the data in the same time.

definition: A fixed set of threads that take work from a queue. If all are busy, new work waits; a slow dependency can exhaust the pool.
example: At 2,000 req/s and 400 ms each, a 300-thread pool is overwhelmed.

definition: A set of open database connections reused across requests, so each request does not pay to open a new one. Too small and requests wait; too large and the database is overloaded.
example: 5,000 queries/s at 4 ms each need about 20 connections from the pool.

definition: Isolating resources (such as a separate thread pool) per dependency, so one slow dependency cannot use up everything and sink the whole service.
example: Giving the recommendations call its own 20-thread pool keeps checkout threads free when it stalls.

definition: A failure in one component that overloads others, which then fail too, spreading through the system.
example: A slow database exhausts app thread pools, which makes the load balancer's health checks fail.

definition: Files served unchanged to every user (images, CSS, JavaScript), ideal for caching on a CDN.
example: Serving static content from a CDN removes it from your servers entirely.

definition: Taking turns in a fixed rotation. A round-robin load balancer sends each new request to the next server in the list; it is simple but ignores how busy each server is.
example: With 4 servers, round-robin sends request 5 back to server 1.

definition: A token carrying the user's identity plus a cryptographic signature, so any server can verify it without looking up a session. Revoking one early is harder.
example: A JWT signed by the auth service lets every app instance check who the user is.

definition: The Redis command that atomically adds 1 to a counter key and returns the new value; used for rate limiting and counters shared by many servers.
example: INCR rl:alice:202510081200 returns 1, 2, 3 ... as Alice's requests arrive.

definition: The Redis command that sets a time-to-live on a key, after which Redis deletes it.
example: EXPIRE key 60 deletes a per-minute rate-limit counter after a minute.

definition: A small program in the Lua language that Redis runs atomically, letting several commands (such as INCR and EXPIRE) happen as one step.
example: A Lua script can increment a counter and set its expiry with no gap between.

definition: What a check does when it cannot work: failing open lets requests through, failing closed blocks them. A rate limiter whose Redis is down must choose one.
example: A rate limiter that fails open keeps the site up but stops limiting during the outage.

definition: A named setting given to a process by its environment at start-up, commonly used to pass configuration without changing code.
example: DATABASE_URL in an environment variable tells every instance where the database is.

definition: Stopping new traffic to an instance and letting its existing requests or connections finish before shutting it down.
example: Draining a WebSocket server moves its users to others before it is replaced.

definition: When adding nodes makes total throughput fall, usually because coordination costs grow faster than capacity.
example: Throughput of 18k req/s at 8 nodes dropping to 15k at 16 is retrograde scaling.

definition: Microsoft's relational database product.
example: Stack Overflow long ran on a handful of powerful SQL Server machines.

definition: A group of networked machines (nodes) that work together as one system, such as a database or cache cluster.
example: A 5-node etcd cluster keeps working while 3 nodes can talk to each other.

definition: A program that processes a large set of data in one run, rather than handling requests one at a time as they arrive.
example: A nightly batch job aggregates the day's clicks into reports.

definition: A chain of processing steps that moves data from where it is produced to where it is stored or analysed.
example: Click events flow through Kafka into a pipeline that updates analytics tables.

definition: A design where each node has its own memory and storage and nodes share nothing but the network, so they can be added independently.
example: Twelve-factor processes share nothing; state lives in backing services.

definition: Quick, rounded arithmetic that tells you the order of magnitude of traffic, storage, bandwidth or servers a design needs, so you can choose components sensibly.
example: 200 M users × 2 posts a day ÷ 100,000 s ≈ 4,000 posts per second.

definition: An estimation question answered by breaking it into simple factors you can guess reasonably, as physicist Enrico Fermi liked to do. Back-of-the-envelope system sizing is a Fermi problem.
example: How many piano tuners are in Chicago? is the classic Fermi problem.

definition: How many copies of each piece of data a store keeps. Storage needed is raw size multiplied by it; 3 is a common choice.
example: 6 TB of records with replication factor 3 needs 18 TB of disk.

definition: How long data is kept before it is deleted or archived. Storage grows with it.
example: Keeping 400 GB a day for 5 years means 730 TB per copy.

definition: A database that stores values under unique keys and looks them up by key, with little or no querying beyond that. Simple and easy to scale out.
example: Mapping short codes to long URLs fits a key-value store perfectly.

definition: AWS's managed key-value and document database. It scales automatically, charges by read and write capacity, and offers eventually consistent or strongly consistent reads.
example: A strongly consistent DynamoDB read of a 4 KB item costs one read capacity unit.

definition: Data leaving a server, datacentre or cloud towards users or other networks. Clouds usually charge for it per GB.
example: Serving 1 PB of photos a day is roughly 80–90 Gbps of egress on average.

definition: Data arriving into a server or network, such as user uploads.
example: 500,000 uploads of 100 MB a day is about 4.6 Gbps of ingress.

definition: High-definition video, usually 720p or 1080p resolution. A minute of it is roughly tens of megabytes depending on compression.
example: A 5 Mbps HD stream uses about 37.5 MB per minute.

definition: How many bits per second a video stream uses. Total streaming bandwidth is viewers multiplied by bitrate.
example: 1 M viewers at 5 Mbps average bitrate need 5 Tbps.

definition: A server close to users (often inside or near their ISP) that caches and serves content, so traffic need not cross the internet from a central datacentre.
example: An edge server in Manchester serves a popular video to local viewers.

definition: Netflix's own content delivery network: storage appliances placed inside ISPs' networks that serve Netflix video locally.
example: Open Connect appliances let most Netflix traffic stay inside the viewer's ISP.

definition: A company that connects homes and businesses to the internet, such as a broadband or mobile provider.
example: Placing caches inside ISPs cuts the distance video has to travel.

definition: A measure of processing work: one CPU core busy for one second. CPU time is the processing a job actually uses, counted this way, as opposed to elapsed time. Work arriving per second, in CPU-seconds, equals the cores you keep busy.
example: 50,000 requests/s × 20 ms of CPU each = 1,000 CPU-seconds per second.

definition: Stating a result with more digits than the inputs justify, which hides how rough the estimate is.
example: "4,629.6 QPS" from guessed inputs is false precision; "about 5k" is honest.

definition: A large chunk of binary data such as an image, video or file. Blobs belong in object storage, with only a reference in the database.
example: A 2 MB photo is a blob; its 1 KB metadata row is not.

definition: Data describing other data: a photo's owner, size, upload time and storage location, rather than the photo's pixels.
example: A 1 KB metadata row per photo is 1 GB a day for a million uploads.

definition: Memory where the operating system or database keeps recently read and written disk pages, so repeat accesses avoid the disk. Writes may sit there before being flushed.
example: Large blobs in a database crowd useful rows out of the buffer cache.

definition: A copy of data saved so it can be restored after loss or corruption. Large databases make backups slow and expensive.
example: Storing photos in Postgres makes every backup carry terabytes of images.

definition: One of several versions of the same image or video at different sizes or qualities, such as a thumbnail, a medium and the full size.
example: A feed mostly loads 20 KB thumbnails, not 2 MB originals.

definition: A way to protect data by splitting it into pieces plus extra parity pieces, so it can be rebuilt from a subset. Uses less disk than keeping full replicas.
example: A 6+3 erasure code survives losing any 3 of 9 pieces with 1.5x storage instead of 3x.

definition: Removing an item from a cache (or a page from memory) to make room for new ones when it is full, according to a policy such as LRU (least recently used).
example: A cache run at 100% of its memory evicts constantly and its hit rate falls.

definition: Filling a cache before (or as) it takes traffic so early requests do not all miss. A cold cache sends almost every request to the database.
example: Warming a replacement cache before switching traffic avoids a stampede on the database.

definition: In a sharded store such as a Redis cluster, the node that holds the authoritative copy of a shard's keys and accepts writes, with replicas copying it.
example: 6 primary shards of 32 GB plus one replica each need 384 GB of memory.

definition: Everyday physical devices (sensors, meters, appliances) connected to the internet and sending data.
example: 10 million IoT sensors each reporting every 10 s produce a million writes a second.

definition: A database optimised for timestamped measurements arriving in order, such as sensor readings or metrics.
example: Device readings with a device ID and timestamp go into a time-series store.

definition: A time-limited URL, signed by your server, that lets a client upload or download one object directly to or from object storage without going through your app servers.
example: The app hands the phone a presigned URL and the 100 MB video goes straight to S3.

definition: Converting a video or audio file into other formats, resolutions or bitrates, so it plays well on many devices and connections.
example: An uploaded 4K video is transcoded into 1080p, 720p and 480p versions.

definition: The hardware that connects a server to the network. Its speed (such as 10 Gbps) caps how much data the server can send or receive.
example: A 10 Gbps NIC can push at most about 1.25 GB/s.

definition: The protocol that addresses and routes packets between machines across the internet. TCP runs on top of it, so the pair is often called TCP/IP; their headers add a few per cent of overhead.
example: Each 1,500-byte packet spends about 40 bytes on TCP/IP headers.

definition: A NoSQL database that stores rows of flexible columns grouped by a partition key, spread across many nodes, such as Cassandra or HBase. Good for huge, write-heavy datasets.
example: Chat messages keyed by channel and time suit a wide-column store.

definition: A class of storage with its own price and speed, from fast and expensive (SSD) to slow and cheap (archive). Old, rarely read data is moved down the tiers.
example: Moving year-old messages to an archive tier cuts their storage cost sharply.

definition: A rule that automatically moves or deletes stored objects as they age, for example to an archive tier after 90 days.
example: An S3 lifecycle policy deletes logs after a year.

definition: A network failure that splits nodes into groups that cannot exchange messages, while each group may keep running. From inside, it looks the same as the other nodes being slow or dead.
example: A cut link between London and Virginia partitions a two-region cluster.

definition: In the CAP theorem, a system's ability to keep operating when the network drops arbitrary messages between nodes. For any system spread over a network it is not optional.
example: Because partitions will happen, the real CAP choice is between consistency and availability during one.

definition: Short for Consistency, Availability and Partition tolerance, the three properties in the CAP theorem. In the theorem, C means linearisability, A means every request to a non-failing node gets a non-error response, and P means tolerating dropped messages between nodes.
example: CAP says that during a network partition a system cannot be both linearisable and available.

definition: Shorthand for what a system gives up during a partition: CP keeps consistency and refuses some requests; AP stays available and may return stale data; CA means it does not handle partitions at all (in practice, a single node).
example: A Raft cluster is CP: its minority side refuses writes during a partition.

definition: An extension of CAP by Daniel Abadi: if there is a Partition, choose Availability or Consistency; Else, even in normal operation, choose Latency or Consistency.
example: Cassandra with ONE reads and writes is PA/EL; Spanner is PC/EC.

definition: Two-part PACELC labels: PA or PC says what a system favours during a partition (availability or consistency); EL or EC says what it favours normally (latency or consistency).
example: A multi-region database that waits for a cross-region quorum on every write is EC.

definition: A group containing more than half the members of a fixed replica set. Any two such groups overlap; protocols such as Raft combine that property with election and log rules to prevent conflicting committed histories. Intersection alone is not the complete correctness protocol.
example: In a 5-node cluster the majority is 3; a 2-node side cannot form one.

definition: An open-source, strongly consistent key-value store that uses Raft. Kubernetes stores its cluster state in it.
example: etcd serves linearisable reads by default by confirming with a quorum.

definition: An open-source coordination service (configuration, locks, leader election) that commits writes through a quorum using the Zab protocol; by default its reads can be slightly stale.
example: Kafka long used ZooKeeper to store cluster metadata.

definition: ZooKeeper Atomic Broadcast: the consensus protocol ZooKeeper uses to order and commit writes through a majority, similar in spirit to Paxos and Raft.
example: Zab makes every ZooKeeper server apply writes in the same order.

definition: Google's globally distributed, strongly consistent SQL database. It uses Paxos replication and TrueTime clocks, and pays commit latency for consistency.
example: Spanner advertises 99.999% availability for multi-region configurations.

definition: An open-source distributed SQL database inspired by Spanner, using Raft replication to stay strongly consistent across nodes and regions.
example: A CockroachDB cluster across three regions survives losing one.

definition: Google's clock API, backed by GPS receivers and atomic clocks, that reports the time with a bounded uncertainty. Spanner waits out that uncertainty to order transactions globally.
example: Spanner waits out the TrueTime uncertainty, typically a few milliseconds, before confirming a commit.

definition: Spanner's guarantee that transactions appear in an order consistent with real time: if one commits before another starts, it is ordered first. Stronger than linearisability for multi-object transactions.
example: Under external consistency a transaction started after yours finished always sees your writes.

definition: An open-source wide-column database modelled on Google's Bigtable, running on Hadoop. It prefers consistency over availability.
example: HBase serves each row from a single region server, so reads are consistent.

definition: A popular open-source document database storing JSON-like documents, with leader-based replica sets.
example: People often label MongoDB "CP", though its guarantees depend on its read and write concerns.

definition: The single replica that accepts writes for some data and sends them to followers. If it fails, a follower is promoted.
example: A Raft cluster elects a new leader when the old one stops sending heartbeats.

definition: A replica that copies writes from the leader. Reading from it is cheaper but may return stale data.
example: A ZooKeeper follower may serve a value a few milliseconds old.

definition: A failure where both sides of a partition believe they are in charge and accept conflicting writes. Majority quorums prevent it.
example: Two primaries accepting writes for the same account is split-brain.

definition: A read that returns an older value than the latest completed write, typically from a lagging replica or cache.
example: Reading a profile from an async replica just after editing it can return the stale version.

definition: Letting the client choose, per request, how many replicas must answer, trading latency and availability against consistency.
example: Cassandra lets each query pick ONE, QUORUM or ALL.

definition: How many replicas must respond for a Cassandra read or write to succeed: ONE (any one), QUORUM (a majority, ⌊replication factor / 2⌋ + 1) or ALL.
example: With replication factor 3, QUORUM means 2 replicas.

definition: When a completed write acknowledgement group and a later read group use the same fixed replica set, their sizes exceeding the replica count forces intersection. This alone does not guarantee the latest value or linearisability: concurrent updates, timestamps and partly applied writes still matter.
example: With 3 replicas, writing to 2 and reading from 2 always overlaps.

definition: Cassandra's compare-and-set operation, implemented with Paxos, that gives linearisable conditional updates at extra latency.
example: INSERT ... IF NOT EXISTS uses a lightweight transaction to claim a username once.

definition: The DynamoDB request flag that asks for a strongly consistent read, which reflects every earlier successful write, at twice the read-capacity cost of an eventually consistent read.
example: GetItem with ConsistentRead=true always reflects the latest successful write.

definition: DynamoDB's billing unit for reads: one strongly consistent read per second of an item up to 4 KB, or two eventually consistent ones.
example: 100,000 eventually consistent reads/s of small items need 50,000 RCUs.

definition: A DynamoDB feature that replicates a table across several AWS Regions. The usual mode replicates asynchronously; AWS also offers a multi-Region strong consistency mode that pays cross-region latency.
example: A global table lets users in Sydney and Virginia both write locally.

definition: A consistency model where operations that are causally related (one could have influenced the other) are seen by everyone in the same order; unrelated ones may be seen in different orders. It can stay available during partitions.
example: Under causal consistency nobody sees a reply before the message it answers.

definition: A guarantee that after you write something, your own later reads see it, even if other users might still see the old value briefly.
example: After editing your profile, you are routed to the primary so you see the change.

definition: A consistency guarantee that reads are never older than a stated limit, in time or number of versions.
example: "Reads may be up to 1 s stale" is a bounded-staleness promise.

definition: A per-replica counter list attached to each version of data, which shows whether one version descends from another or whether they were written concurrently.
example: Version vectors reveal that {book, pen} and {book, mug} are concurrent cart versions that need merging.

definition: A data structure designed so replicas can be updated independently and always merged automatically into the same result, without conflicts.
example: A grow-only counter CRDT sums each replica's count, so concurrent increments are never lost.

definition: A set CRDT that tags every add with a unique id; a remove deletes only the tags it has seen, so a concurrent new add survives (add wins) and removed items do not reappear.
example: An OR-Set cart stops a deleted item coming back when two cart versions merge.

definition: A conflict rule that keeps the version with the latest timestamp and silently discards the other, losing concurrent updates and trusting clocks.
example: Under LWW, one of two concurrent cart additions simply vanishes.

definition: The difference between clocks on different machines. It makes timestamps from different servers unreliable for deciding which event happened first.
example: With 50 ms of clock skew, an earlier write can carry the later timestamp and win under LWW.

definition: Writes made without either writer having seen the other, so neither version descends from the other and they must be merged or one discarded.
example: Two sides of a partition both updating a cart produce concurrent versions.

definition: A ZooKeeper call that makes the client's server catch up with the leader before the next read; it improves freshness but is not a quorum operation or a strict linearisability guarantee.
example: Calling sync() before reading a flag makes a stale answer much less likely.
