definition: A configuration switch that turns a feature on or off at run time without deploying new code.
example: Flipping a feature flag enables the new checkout for 5% of users.

definition: How far a replica is behind the primary, in time or in writes. Reads from a lagging replica are stale.
example: A replica 2 s behind will not show a profile edit made a second ago.

definition: A point in a database's write log (in Postgres, an LSN). Recording the position of a user's write lets you read from a replica only once it has replayed that far.
example: Read from the replica once its replayed LSN passes the user's last write.

definition: An automated teller machine. Brewer's example of choosing availability during a partition: it keeps dispensing up to a limit and reconciles later.
example: A disconnected ATM allowing £200 per card logs withdrawals to settle when the link returns.

definition: Comparing and correcting records after a period of independent operation, such as settling offline transactions once connectivity returns.
example: After the partition heals, the bank reconciles ATM logs against the ledger.

definition: A database setting that controls how much concurrent transactions can see of each other's uncommitted or recent work, trading safety against performance.
example: Serializable isolation behaves as if transactions ran one at a time.

definition: Eric Brewer's 2000 claim that a networked shared-data system cannot be consistent, available and partition-tolerant at once; Seth Gilbert and Nancy Lynch proved a formal version in 2002, turning it into the CAP theorem.
example: Gilbert and Lynch defined C as linearisability in their proof.

definition: A short document recording one architectural decision: its context, the decision and its consequences, so future engineers know why and when to revisit it.
example: An ADR notes "chose async replication; revisit if we add live auctions".

definition: The operating-system call that forces data a program has written out of memory buffers onto durable storage. Until it returns, a power cut can lose the data.
example: A database commit is durable only once its log record has been fsynced.

definition: The software that manages a computer's hardware and runs programs, such as Linux. It buffers disk writes in memory before flushing them.
example: With appendfsync no, the OS decides when Redis's writes reach disk.

definition: The PostgreSQL setting for when a commit is acknowledged: on waits for the WAL to be flushed (and for synchronous standbys if configured); off acknowledges first and can lose the last moments of commits in a crash, but never corrupts data. It can be set per transaction.
example: SET synchronous_commit = off for click logging trades a fraction of a second of possible loss for speed.

definition: How often PostgreSQL's background WAL writer flushes the log, 200 ms by default. With asynchronous commit, a crash can lose up to about three times this.
example: At the 200 ms default, the asynchronous-commit risk window is about 600 ms.

definition: A synchronous_commit level that waits until a synchronous standby has applied the commit, so reads on the standby see it immediately.
example: With remote_apply, a read routed to the standby right after a commit sees the new row.

definition: The Kafka producer setting for how many replicas must confirm a write before it counts: 0 (none), 1 (leader only) or all (all in-sync replicas). Default all since Kafka 3.0.
example: With acks=1, a leader crash before followers copy an event loses it.

definition: The Kafka topic setting for the minimum number of in-sync replicas that must hold a write for acks=all to succeed. It defaults to 1; 2 with 3 replicas tolerates one replica loss.
example: With min.insync.replicas=2, writes are rejected if only one replica is in sync.

definition: In Kafka, a follower that is keeping up with the partition leader. Only in-sync replicas count towards acks=all.
example: A follower that falls 30 s behind drops out of the in-sync replica set.

definition: A Kafka producer mode that tags messages with sequence numbers so retries do not create duplicates in a partition. On by default since Kafka 3.0.
example: A retried send after a timeout is written once, not twice.

definition: The Kafka producer setting for how long to wait to fill a batch before sending. Higher values mean bigger batches and more throughput, at the cost of per-message latency. Default 5 ms since Kafka 4.0.
example: Raising linger.ms from 5 to 50 sends ten times fewer, larger batches.

definition: A program that writes messages or events to a broker such as Kafka.
example: The order service is a producer of order-created events.

definition: A program that reads messages or events from a broker such as Kafka, tracking its position (offset) as it goes.
example: The email service is a consumer of order-created events.

definition: The position in a Kafka partition up to which a consumer has processed messages. After a crash it resumes from its last committed offset.
example: A consumer restarted at offset 1,042 reprocesses nothing before it.

definition: One ordered, append-only log within a Kafka topic. Partitions spread a topic over brokers and set how many consumers can read in parallel; ordering holds only within one.
example: A topic with 12 partitions can be read by up to 12 consumers in a group at once.

definition: Letting Kafka consumers read from a nearby follower replica instead of always from the leader, which cuts cross-zone traffic.
example: A consumer in zone B reads from the zone-B follower rather than the zone-A leader.

definition: Redis persistence that periodically writes a point-in-time snapshot of the whole dataset to disk. Everything since the last snapshot is lost in a crash.
example: With RDB every 5 minutes, a crash can lose up to 5 minutes of writes.

definition: Redis persistence that logs every write command to a file and replays it on restart. How often it is fsynced (appendfsync) sets how much can be lost.
example: With AOF and appendfsync everysec, a power cut loses about a second of writes.

definition: The Redis setting for how often the append-only file is fsynced: always (every write, slowest, safest), everysec (about once a second, the usual choice) or no (leave it to the OS).
example: appendfsync everysec is fast and loses about a second of writes at worst in normal operation.

definition: A Redis tool that checks an append-only file and can truncate an incomplete final command so the file loads again.
example: After a power cut, redis-check-aof --fix trims a half-written last command.

definition: Making many transactions durable with a single fsync of the log, so the cost of one disk flush is shared. It raises throughput at the cost of some waiting per commit.
example: At 2 ms per fsync, batching 50 commits lifts the ceiling from 500 to 25,000 commits/s.

definition: A TCP feature that holds back small packets briefly to combine them into bigger ones, saving bandwidth but adding latency. Interactive apps often disable it with the TCP_NODELAY option.
example: A game server sets TCP_NODELAY so each small update goes out immediately.

definition: What a cloud provider charges for data moving between zones, regions or out to the internet, usually per GB. Chatty cross-zone designs can spend more on it than on compute.
example: 0.67 TB a day of cross-zone calls is billed every day it flows.

definition: Sending each call to an instance in the caller's own availability zone when one is healthy, falling back to other zones only when needed, to cut latency and transfer costs.
example: With 3 zones, zone-aware routing removes most of the two-thirds of calls that would cross zones.

definition: Running more capacity than average load needs, to cover peaks and failures. It costs money when idle; too little causes outages.
example: Running 75 servers for a load 45 would carry is deliberate over-provisioning for an AZ loss.

definition: A SQL clause that locks the rows it selects and skips rows other transactions have already locked, letting many workers safely take different jobs from one table.
example: Workers running SELECT ... FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED LIMIT 1 each grab a different job.

definition: A list of tasks waiting to be processed by background workers, such as sending emails or resizing images.
example: Checkout adds "email ticket" to a job queue and returns immediately.

definition: Complexity that comes from the problem itself and cannot be designed away, as opposed to accidental complexity.
example: Handling partial refunds is essential complexity in a payments system.

definition: Complexity introduced by our tools and design choices rather than by the problem, which a simpler design could avoid.
example: Running 12 microservices for a seven-person team adds accidental complexity.

definition: Amazon's terms for decisions that are hard to reverse (one-way doors, such as data models or public APIs) versus cheap to reverse (two-way doors, such as a cache TTL). Spend careful thought on the first kind.
example: A public API shape is a one-way door; a config value is a two-way door.

definition: The decision whether to create a component yourself or use a vendor's product or managed service, weighed on differentiation, expertise, time, scale and control.
example: Buying managed search makes sense for a 6-person start-up; building may at 50 PB.

definition: Hard work every company must do that gives no competitive advantage, such as running databases or queues. A strong case for managed services.
example: Patching your own Elasticsearch cluster is undifferentiated heavy lifting.

definition: Depending on one provider's product so heavily that switching would be very costly.
example: Using a cloud-specific database API increases vendor lock-in.

definition: How easily software can be moved to a different platform or provider. Paying for it you never use is a cost too.
example: Abstracting every cloud service "in case we migrate" buys portability at a price.

definition: A popular distributed search and analytics engine for full-text search and logs, built on Apache Lucene and running on the JVM.
example: Running Elasticsearch well needs care with shard sizes, JVM heap and upgrades.

definition: The runtime that executes Java (and other JVM languages) bytecode, managing memory with a garbage collector. Its heap size must be tuned for services like Elasticsearch and Kafka.
example: A JVM heap that is too large can cause long garbage-collection pauses.

definition: Dropbox's in-house storage system, which by 2015 held about 500 PB and served over 90% of its users' data, after Dropbox moved off Amazon S3 for performance and cost.
example: Dropbox decided that at its scale, building its own storage beat buying it from S3.

definition: Two ways to build feeds: push precomputes each follower's feed when something is posted (fan-out on write); pull assembles a feed when it is read (fan-out on read).
example: Pushing a post to 500 followers' feeds means 500 writes, but each read is cheap.

definition: Short for serialisation and deserialisation: converting data to bytes for the network or disk and back again. It costs CPU time on every call between services.
example: Each microservice hop adds roughly half a millisecond of serde plus the round trip.

definition: Measuring where a program spends its time or memory, function by function, to find what is actually slow before changing anything.
example: Profiling shows 80% of request time is one slow SQL query.

definition: Running several versions of a public API side by side so clients can migrate on their own schedule before the old one is deprecated (announced for removal).
example: Introducing /v2/links and deprecating /v1 over six months is API versioning.

definition: Returning a large list in pages (for example 50 items plus a cursor for the next page) rather than all at once.
example: GET /links?cursor=abc returns the next 50 links.

definition: The value of the best alternative you give up by choosing something, such as the features engineers could have built instead of running infrastructure.
example: Four engineers running a log cluster have an opportunity cost of everything else they could ship.

definition: Availability measured as the fraction of requests that succeeded, rather than the fraction of time the service was up. It weights an outage by how many users it actually hit.
example: 1 million failed requests out of 1 billion is 99.9% request-based availability.

definition: Availability measured as the fraction of time a service was up: uptime divided by total time. It counts a minute down at 3 a.m. the same as a minute down at peak.
example: 43 minutes down in a 43,200-minute month is 99.9% time-based availability.

definition: Resolving conflicting versions of a set by keeping every element that appears in any version. No addition is lost, but an item deleted in one version can reappear.
example: Merging carts {book, pen} and {book, mug} by union gives {book, pen, mug}.
